items.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Wasn’t that the story with Freddie Keppard? ... [INTERVIEWEE] Yeah. Wouldn’t record.

ctx.x: Oh, yeah. And radio, I mean there weren’t the number of people producing stuff for radio. And advertisers didn’t understand how valuable radio was. Musicians didn’t understand how valuable the advertising of having a record was. There were early musicians that wouldn’t record because they were afraid that people would steal their music. So the first people who recorded became insanely popular.
Wasn’t that the story with Freddie Keppard? And he passed up the chance to be the first Dixieland group?

Yeah. Wouldn’t record. But as soon as people began to realize that then to get a record was important if you wanted to be a popular band, and to get a job in a club that had a radio wire at night was important. That was one of the big things that built the bands at the Hickory House. I used to work there with Marian McPartland. But in the years before that, when they were first starting out, at night, they didn’t have a whole lot of sponsored programs. So all the radio stations would put telephone wires into the…
